blocks.title: 1. The Core Concept: The Most Famous Equation in Geometry
blocks.content: Over 2,500 years ago, Pythagoras discovered something magical about right-angled triangles: if you square the two shorter sides and add them together, you get the square of the longest side (the hypotenuse). **a^2 + b^2 = c^2**, where c is always the hypotenuse. This single equation lets you find unknown distances in everything from construction to GPS navigation.

blocks.title: 2. The Rules: Identifying the Hypotenuse
blocks.content:
• The **hypotenuse** is ALWAYS the longest side.
• It ALWAYS sits opposite the right angle (the 90-degree angle).
• In the formula a^2 + b^2 = c^2, **c is always the hypotenuse**.
• The two shorter sides (a and b) are called the 'legs'.
• This theorem ONLY works for right-angled triangles!

blocks.title: 3. Step-by-Step: Finding a Missing Side
blocks.content:
Finding the hypotenuse: c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Finding a leg: a = sqrt(c^2 - b^2).

1. Identify which side is the hypotenuse (longest, opposite the right angle).
2. If finding the hypotenuse: ADD the squares, then square root.
3. If finding a shorter side: SUBTRACT the squares, then square root.
4. Always square root at the end!

blocks.title: 4. Worked Example: Finding the Hypotenuse
blocks.content:
A right triangle has legs of 6cm and 8cm. Find the hypotenuse.

**Step 1:** c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100.
**Step 2:** c = sqrt(100) = 10.

**Final Answer: The hypotenuse is 10cm.**
(This is the famous 3-4-5 triple scaled by 2!)

blocks.title: 5. Common Pitfalls
blocks.content: Two deadly traps: (1) Students add the squares when they should subtract (or vice versa). If you're finding the HYPOTENUSE, you ADD. If you're finding a SHORTER side, you SUBTRACT. (2) Forgetting to square root at the end! If c^2 = 100, the answer is c = 10, NOT c = 100. Always finish with the square root step.
